Report 2: the field-trip signup form will not start, and the language reports it cannot understand line 4, which reads ""IF permission THEN"" with nothing after it. Classify the error.
Incorrect. A logic error runs. This program never starts, which rules the category out immediately.
Incorrect. A run-time error occurs during execution. Execution never began here, because the language could not read the statement.
Correct. The tell is in the report itself: the language cannot understand the line. That is the definition of a broken language rule.
Incorrect. Overflow is about a number outside a defined range. No number is involved.
<div class=""mcq-q-text"">Report 1: GradePro averages print too high for every student, no error message has ever appeared, and the formula reads ""avg &lt
column2: - (q1 + q2 + q3) / 2"". Which phrase in the report gives the classification away?

column1: Incorrect. Sample size tells you the bug is consistent, not what kind of bug it is.
Correct. Running cleanly while producing wrong output is the signature of a logic error. Silence plus wrongness is the pair to look for.
Incorrect. The direction of the error helps you find the cause, but the same classification would hold if averages printed too low.
Incorrect. Division appears in Report 3 as well, where it causes a completely different error type.
Report 3: the bill-splitter worked every lunch period for weeks, then halted mid-run when a user entered 0 diners. Why do weeks of clean runs not contradict the classification?
Correct. Weeks of clean runs prove only that diners was never 0. The defect was present and dormant throughout.
Incorrect. The same path ran every time. What differed was the value flowing through it.
Incorrect. Nothing in the report describes a change. The same legal code sat there the whole time.
Incorrect. Repetition does not age code into failure. The trigger is a particular input, not a run count.
Which test case would have exposed the bill-splitter defect before launch?
Incorrect. Typical values are what already ran cleanly for weeks. They cannot find this.
Incorrect. A hundred typical runs is the situation the report describes. Volume without extremes finds nothing.
Incorrect. A second reader might spot it, but that is not one of the CED's named discovery methods and it is not a test case.
Correct. Zero is the minimum possible party, and the extreme is exactly where the CED's testing rule says to look.
Report 4: a step-count badge reset to 0 exactly as the count passed the counter's defined maximum. Classify the error.
Incorrect. Nothing failed to parse. The program ran all day.
Incorrect. The wrong display is what makes this tempting, but the algorithm was correct. Add one step per step is exactly right.
Correct. The value outgrew the range the computer could represent, which is a separately named failure on the taxonomy.
Incorrect. The timing looks like a run-time error, but the CED gives this specific cause its own name.
Why is Report 4 not classified as a logic error, given that the badge showed a wrong number?
Incorrect. Logic errors are silent. Report 1 is silent too, and it is a logic error.
Correct. This is the distinction the taxonomy turns on. A correct algorithm can still meet a number the storage cannot hold.
Incorrect. Where the wrong number appears does not change what caused it.
Incorrect. Counters can absolutely carry logic errors. This one does not.
<div class=""mcq-q-text"">Report 5: the ""streak!"" celebration sometimes fires after wrong answers, the streak number itself displays correctly, and the check reads ""IF streak &gt
column2: 0"" instead of testing the newest answer. Which method pins down the guilty line?

column1: Correct. The trace shows the condition firing with no test of the newest answer, which localizes the defect to that line.
Incorrect. The report says there is no crash, ever. Waiting for one is waiting forever.
Incorrect. Changing the threshold makes the celebration rarer without ever testing the answer. The defect survives.
Incorrect. A rewrite carries the same wrong condition unless you first find it.
GradePro's formula is fixed to divide by 3 and a test case of q1 = 90, q2 = 80, q3 = 70 expecting 80 is run. It fails anyway. What does the CED's testing loop require next?
Incorrect. Reclassifying changes the label, not the wrong average.
Incorrect. A failing test on a hand-computed expected value is a finding, not noise.
Incorrect. Rewriting the expectation to match the behaviour is how a wrong program passes its own tests forever.
Correct. Test results exist to drive revision. Revise, then re-test, and repeat until the defined input produces the expected outcome.

Scenario 1: a gradebook accepts whole-number scores from 0 to 100. The developer tested 85, 92 and 74, all correct, and wants to ship. What is the red flag?
Incorrect. Independent testing is good practice but is not what the CED faults here.
Incorrect. They can, provided the requirements define which score maps to which letter.
Incorrect. Count is not the issue. Four well-chosen boundary tests beat fifty middle values.
Correct. The CED asks for inputs at or just beyond the extremes, and 74 to 92 is the safe middle of a 0 to 100 range.
Which test set defends the gradebook, and against what?
Incorrect. Even spacing feels thorough but tests the interior. It includes the extremes only by accident and never goes beyond them.
Incorrect. Testing one end leaves the other unguarded, and a program that grades 101 without complaint never crashes to tell you.
Correct. At the extremes, both are legal and must grade correctly. Just beyond, both must be rejected. An off-by-one comparison fails only the 0 test.
Incorrect. Nothing interesting happens at 50. The requirements draw no line there.
Scenario 2: the star rating box is free-type, and the lead developer says the 1 to 5 range ""is obvious, so nobody will type anything else."" How should a tester treat that claim?
Incorrect. A clearer label may reduce mistakes, but a free-type box still accepts every number.
Correct. Nobody will type it is a hope, not a defence. The testing rule points straight at the values just beyond the extremes.
Incorrect. The display constrains the picture, not the field. The box accepts what the box accepts.
Incorrect. Skipping the input the developer swears cannot happen is how the defect ships.
Scenario 2, second layer: a film with zero ratings. Why do star-value tests never meet this defect?
Correct. Sum divided by count is legal code that fails at the minimum of an input nobody was testing. The requirements never define behaviour for that case.
Incorrect. The scenario says the average shows on every film page, which is what makes the empty case reachable.
Incorrect. Nothing in the requirements delays the calculation until some popularity threshold.
Incorrect. Testing a star value of 0 exercises the rating input. It never produces a film with no ratings at all.
Scenario 3: passwords must be 8 to 16 characters, and the intern tested ""sunshine12"" at ten characters. What must a tester name before building the test set?
Incorrect. Load is unrelated to a boundary defined by the requirements.
Incorrect. Passwords are not numbers, and the requirement says nothing about a numeric range.
Incorrect. The allowed characters matter for a different rule. The stated requirement is a length range.
Correct. Naming what is measured is the whole game here. Testing password values instead of password lengths tests the wrong axis entirely.
Scenario 4: a wellness app logs nightly sleep from 0 to 1440 minutes and keeps a lifetime running total in the same size of storage. Where is the overflow risk?
Incorrect. That range governs the nightly input. It says nothing about the total built from it, which is the boundary the requirements forgot.
Incorrect. 1440 is tiny. A nightly value can never approach the limit of the storage.
Correct. A semester at roughly 480 minutes a night approaches 87,000, and the requirements never define a ceiling for the accumulated value at all.
Incorrect. Sharing a storage size is what makes the comparison interesting, but only one of the two grows without bound.
